newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia bonds in correction, debate rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia bonds in correction, debate rate cut.

text.p: *Australian bonds succumbed to a technical correction after its recent hefty rally as a stronger than expected rise in employment then combined with a sharp sell-off in U.S. bonds.
*Market continues to debate possibility of third rate cut.

Australian bonds finally succumbed to a technical correction after its recent hefty two-month rally, triggered by a stronger than expected rise in October employment and then a sharp sell-off in U.S. Treasuries.
The market also continued to debate whether Wednesday's 1/2 point point rate cut by the Reserve Bank to 6.50 percent would be the last in the cycle or if a third easing is possible.

Comments by Japan's senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that the Japanese economy was stronger than the market thought and the yen's correction should be over sent the U.S. dollar into a tailspin and sent U.S. yields up sharply.
The Australian dollar also came under severe pressure as the currency's yield advantage was seen being further eroded if Japan is on the cusp of tightening policy.

The 10-year bond yield spiked up nearly 20 basis points from the 32-month low of around 7.17 percent seen during after hours trading on continued offshore demand, but still stands some 100 basis points below the yield level seen just two months ago.
However, "The rate cut yesterday to 6.5 percent opens the door for bonds to go to 7.0 percent," said Rory Robertson, fixed interest analyst at BT Australia.

"But it's hard to see any dramatic rally past 7.0 percent until you see the (Reserve) Bank acknowledge the weakness in the economy," Robertson added, who believes there was a case for the central bank to have cut rates by 100 basis points yesterday.
He believes there is a 30 to 40 percent chance of a further easing in December.

Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank is pencilling in a cut around next March, while UBS chief economist Stephen Roberts said today's data was not soft enough to suggest any urgent need for the Reserve Bank cut again until it has full advantage of inflation and wages data over the next 3-4 months.
Employment rose 25,500 in October against median forecasts for a 12,000 rise, although the unemployment rate sneaked up to 8.8 percent when it was expected to remain at 8.7 percent.

"The number was higher than widely expected and marks a sharp rebound from the 34,000 fall in September. If employment gains continued at or above this rate over the next three months, the chance of another rate cut in February would be zero," said John Edwards, chief economist at Societe Generale.
Bond yield spreads generally reversed there initially tightening trend, although the Australian/U.S. 10-year spread remained just below 100 basis points.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasuries face the last leg of the refunding auctions with a US$10 billion 30-year bond auction.
